summary: Summarizes the requirements for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting protocols for network access, as criteria for evaluating candidates. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Any protocol that checks a user's identity, decides what they may do and records what they used has to satisfy several groups at once. RFC 2989 merges the requirements those groups had written separately into one list, so that a proposed protocol can be judged against it.

subtitle: One checklist for judging a protocol that checks users in, says what they may do and bills them

tldr.problem: Protocols for network access have to satisfy several groups at once, and each of those groups had written its own requirements, so there was no single list to judge a proposed protocol against.
tldr.mechanism: The memo merges the requirements from the NASREQ, ROAMOPS and MOBILE IP working groups and from TIA 45.6 into four lists, general, authentication, authorization and accounting, with the level each source group demands and a note explaining each requirement.
tldr.outcome: The result is a checklist rather than a protocol. It also fixes the language for judging one: a submission that misses a must is not compliant, one that misses only the shoulds is conditionally compliant, and one that meets everything is unconditionally compliant.

today: RFC 2989 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a summary of other people's requirements, with the detail left in the documents it refers to, so it reads as a snapshot of what the access protocol world wanted at the time.

sections.title: What This Memo Is
sections.content:
The memo summarises the requirements for Authentication, Authorization and Accounting protocols used for network access. Its inputs came from documents produced by the Network Access Server Requirements Next Generation (NASREQ), Roaming Operations (ROAMOPS) and MOBILEIP working groups, and from TIA 45.6. It collects those requirements and separates them into authentication, authorization and accounting, and it points readers to the original documents for the detail.

The requirement words are used as in RFC 2119. The memo is careful about what they mean here: the requirements describe capabilities of a protocol, and the protocol document itself decides whether a given feature is required, recommended or optional. Requiring that a protocol support confidentiality is not the same thing as requiring that all protocol traffic be encrypted.

That gives a way to judge a submission. A protocol submission is not compliant if it fails one or more of the must or must-not requirements for the capabilities it implements. A submission that satisfies all the must and must-not requirements but not all the should or should-not ones is conditionally compliant, and one that satisfies them all is unconditionally compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: Several groups each wrote down what they wanted from an access protocol, in their own words. This memo merges them into one checklist so that a new protocol can be judged the same way by everyone. It also says what the requirement words mean: a protocol that fails a must is not compliant, and one that misses only the shoulds is conditionally compliant.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
An administrative domain is an internet, or a collection of networks, computers and databases under a common administration; entities in one administration may be assumed to share administratively created security associations. A client is a node wishing to obtain service from an attendant, and an attendant is a node providing the service interface between a client and the local domain.

Three kinds of middleman appear in the definitions. A proxy acts as both a client and a server: it is a server to the node that sent the request and a client when it forwards the same request on. A local proxy is a proxy that lives in the same administrative domain as the network device that issued the request; it typically enforces local policies before forwarding responses and is generally used to multiplex AAA messages from a large number of network devices. A transparent proxy is a proxy that enforces no local policy, meaning it does not add, delete or modify attributes or modify information in the messages it forwards. A broker sits in a third administrative domain, different from both the home AAA server and the local ISP, and provides services such as facilitating payments between them, and there are two kinds. A proxy broker is a transparent proxy that acts as the forwarding agent for all AAA messages between the local ISP and the home domain's servers. A routing broker is not in the transmission path at all: it returns information that lets the requester contact the home AAA server directly, and it may also act as a certificate authority so that the local ISP and the home servers can communicate securely.

The rest of the vocabulary covers the accounting and roaming sides. Accounting is collecting information on resource usage for trend analysis, auditing, billing or cost allocation, and it is intra-domain when the packets and session records stay inside one administrative domain and inter-domain when they cross administrative boundaries. Real-time accounting processes that information within a defined time window, typically imposed to limit financial risk. A session record summarises the resource consumption of a user over the whole session, and accounting gateways may build one by processing interim accounting events. Roaming capability is the ability to use any one of several providers while keeping a formal customer relationship with only one. The Network Access Identifier is the user ID submitted during network access authentication; in roaming it identifies the user and helps route the request, and it need not match an email address or an application-layer user ID.

Two security models are defined, and they matter for the requirements that follow. End-to-end means security information can traverse, and still be validated after, intermediate nodes such as proxies and brokers. Hop-by-hop means each direct pair of peers shares a security association and the security information does not traverse an AAA entity. The memo also defines home, foreign and local domains for Mobile IP: the foreign domain is the one a Mobile IP client visits, and the local domain is the one of immediate interest to it while it is away from home.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary matters because the requirements are about messages passing through other people's servers. A proxy is a server to the device that asks and a client to the server it forwards to. A broker sits in a third organisation and either forwards the messages or just hands out the information needed to reach the home server directly. The Network Access Identifier is the name the user dials in with, and in roaming it also says where the request should go.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
The general requirements apply to all of AAA. A protocol must be able to support millions of users and tens of thousands of simultaneous requests, and the architecture and protocol must support tens of thousands of devices, AAA servers, proxies and brokers. When a server cannot be reached, the protocol must offer a way to move service to a backup or secondary server. Mutual authentication between the AAA client and server must be possible.

Two security models are required at different levels. Transmission level security, also called hop-by-hop security, means authentication, integrity protection and confidentiality between two communicating peers, and all of the security is removed when the message is processed by the receiving AAA entity. Object level confidentiality means that only the entity the data is ultimately destined for can decrypt it, even if the message passes through proxies or brokers. Object level integrity means the same for authentication and integrity protection, and because the authentication must persist across intermediate entities, data covered by it cannot be modified by them. The protocol must be able to transport certificates, which is meant as an optimisation in lieu of fetching them out of band.

A reliable transport mechanism is required too, covering resilience against packet loss: hop-by-hop retransmission and fail-over so reliability does not depend on a single hop, control of the retransmission mechanism by the AAA application, an acknowledgement from the transport that a message was delivered successfully as distinct from the message semantics, piggy-backing of acknowledgements in AAA messages, and timely delivery of responses. The protocol must run over IPv4 and over IPv6, and must support proxy and routing brokers.

Three further general requirements are listed. Auditability means it is possible to determine definitively what actions were performed on AAA packets as they travel from the home AAA server to the network device and back. The protocol must allow communication to be secured, but it must also allow an underlying security service such as IP Security to be used, in which case its own security must not be required. And it must be extensible by third parties, so that groups other than the AAA working group can define standard attributes for the service they are specifying. Four of the general requirements are marked as must by all three source groups: scalability, data object confidentiality, data object integrity, and running over IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The general rules apply to every part of the system. The protocol has to cope with millions of users, survive a server going away, run over both IP versions, and be able to carry attributes that other groups define. On security it asks for two different things: each hop protected on its own, and the payload protected so that only the server it is really meant for can read it, even if proxies handle it on the way.

sections.title: Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
Six authentication requirements are listed. The protocol must allow the use of Network Access Identifiers to identify users and devices. It must be able to transport CHAP authentication information, which is what network access servers commonly use when they request authentication of a PPP user. It must be able to transport EAP payloads, and since some EAP mechanisms need more than one round trip the protocol must allow them; the actual EAP mechanism negotiated must be transparent to the AAA protocol, and when EAP is used authentication typically happens between the user and their home AAA server.

Clear-text passwords still have to be supported, even though PAP is deprecated, because it remains in widespread use for its original purpose of clear-text passwords. The protocol therefore has to transport clear-text passwords securely, which means providing confidentiality for clear-text passwords travelling over the wire and protecting against disclosure of them to proxies in the forwarding path.

Two requirements cover what happens later. A user must be able to be re-authenticated on demand, and the event can be triggered by the user, by the access device acting as the AAA client, or by the home or visited AAA server. And the protocol must not require the user's credentials during authorization: authorization is supported by identification or assertion alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has to carry several kinds of proof of identity, including the challenge-and-response used by PPP users, the extensible protocol EAP, and, though it is on the way out, plain passwords, which therefore have to be protected in transit and hidden from any proxy on the way. It must also allow a user to be checked again on demand, and it must not insist on the password again at the authorization stage.

sections.title: Authorization Requirements
sections.content:
Authorization covers what the user is then allowed to do. A server must be able to provide a static or dynamic address during the authorization phase, of type IPv4 or IPv6; if both the client and the server know a pre-configured address it counts as static and anything else is dynamic. The protocol must be able to accommodate the large installed base of attributes for existing approaches such as RADIUS, so that a server implementation could speak both protocols or translate between them. A proxy broker must be able to deny access without forwarding the request to the AAA server at all, or to deny access after receiving an access accept from it. The protocol must not preclude layer 2 tunnelling.

Four requirements concern how authorization evolves. Re-authorization on demand means the AAA client or server can trigger it, or the server can send updated authorization information to the device, such as a stop service message; an authorization can carry a time limit, so a server can let a user in and later decide the user is no longer allowed to use the service, and re-authorization does not necessarily imply re-authentication. The protocol must be able to describe access operational limitations and authorization restrictions to the NAS, including session expirations and idle timeouts, packet filters, static routes and QoS parameters.

State reconciliation lets the NAS use the AAA server to manage resource allocation state, which assists with but is not the same as simultaneous user login control, port usage limitations or IP address pooling. The design must provide for recovery from data loss caused by NAS and AAA server reboots and by communication outages, and it must be independent of the accounting stream, with the granularity of recovery possibly on the order of a fraction of a minute, which means explicit session and resource status, update and disconnect messages. Because of potential multi-domain issues, only systems that allocate or use a resource should track its state. Finally, unsolicited disconnect lets the AAA server ask the NAS to disconnect an active session for authorization policy reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the user is known, the protocol has to say what they get: an address, static or dynamic, in either IP version. It must be able to refuse access without troubling the home server, and it must carry the details of the session, such as filters, routes and how long the session lasts. The AAA server must also be able to change its mind later and cut the session off, and the system must be able to rebuild its picture of who is connected after a crash without relying on the billing records.

sections.title: Accounting Requirements
sections.content:
Accounting has to be close to real time. The requirement may be loosely defined as reporting synchronously with events, and the time window is typically on the order of seconds rather than milliseconds. The accounting data format must not be bloated, imposing a large overhead for one or more accounting data elements. The accounting record format must be extensible, so that new metrics can be added, and it must support both standard metrics and vendor-specific metrics. Batch accounting, where several records are buffered or stored and sent together later, is listed as a should. Delivery must be guaranteed, and this is an application layer acknowledgement sent when the receiving server is willing to take responsibility for the message data. Time stamps must reflect the time of occurrence of events such as log-on, logoff, authentication, authorization and interim accounting, and must be unambiguous. Dynamic accounting covers the case where authentication and authorization happen during the session, so that a single session can have multiple accounting records.

Mobile IP adds three requirements of its own: the encoding of Mobile IP registration messages must be carried, the protocol must be firewall friendly, meaning designed to accommodate a firewall acting as a proxy so that a home agent AAA server behind a firewall can be reached from the Internet to provide AAA services to a Mobile IP foreign agent, and the allocation of a local home agent is required to some degree.

The memo closes by saying that, being a requirements document, it has no security concerns of its own, since the security requirements on the protocols being evaluated are described in the documents it refers to, and that it creates no new number spaces for IANA administration.
sections.plainLanguage: The billing side has to be nearly live: the system should report what a session used as it happens, not days later. Records must be small, must be able to grow new fields later, and must be acknowledged by the server that takes responsibility for them. Every event needs an unambiguous time stamp.

viz.caption: THE REQUIREMENT WORDS AND WHAT THEY MEAN

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Required. A submission that fails a must or must-not requirement is not compliant.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: Recommended. Missing one makes a submission conditionally compliant.

items.title: Network access server
items.text: The device the user dials in to; it acts as the AAA client.

items.title: Local proxy
items.text: A proxy in the same administrative domain as the access device, applying local policy and multiplexing messages.

items.title: Proxy broker
items.text: A transparent proxy in a third organisation that forwards all AAA messages between the local ISP and the home server.

items.title: Routing broker
items.text: A broker outside the message path; it returns the information needed to reach the home server directly.

items.title: Home AAA server
items.text: The server in the domain that holds the user's account.

items.title: Foreign AAA server
items.text: The server in the domain a Mobile IP client is visiting.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: THE PATH OF AN AAA REQUEST THROUGH A PROXY CHAIN

messages.label: AAA REQUEST
messages.note: The access device asks for the user to be authenticated or authorized.

messages.label: FORWARDED
messages.note: A proxy forwards the request to the home AAA server.

messages.label: REPLY
messages.note: The home server answers, and the answer travels back the same way.

messages.label: AAA REPLY
messages.note: The local server returns the decision and the attributes for the session.
